claim: Mutant KRAS colorectal cancer (CRC) cells release protein-laden exosomes that can alter the tumor microenvironment.
source: Mutant KRAS colorectal cancer (CRC) cells release protein-laden exosomes that can alter the tumor microenvironment.
evidence: This statement is presented in the abstract as an established finding, supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Exosomal profiles are distinct from cellular profiles.
source: We show that exosomal profiles are distinct from cellular profiles, and mutant exosomes cluster separately from wild-type KRAS exosomes.
evidence: This claim is supported by principal component analysis and correlation data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Mutant exosomes cluster separately from wild-type KRAS exosomes.
source: We show that exosomal profiles are distinct from cellular profiles, and mutant exosomes cluster separately from wild-type KRAS exosomes.
evidence: This is demonstrated through principal component analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: miR-10b was selectively increased in wild-type exosomes.
source: miR-10b was selectively increased in wild-type exosomes, while miR-100 was increased in mutant exosomes.
evidence: This is supported by RNA sequencing data and qRT-PCR validation.

claim: miR-100 was increased in mutant exosomes.
source: miR-10b was selectively increased in wild-type exosomes, while miR-100 was increased in mutant exosomes.
evidence: This is supported by RNA sequencing data and qRT-PCR validation.

claim: Neutral sphingomyelinase inhibition caused accumulation of miR-100 only in mutant cells.
source: Neutral sphingomyelinase inhibition caused accumulation of miR-100 only in mutant cells, suggesting KRAS-dependent miRNA export.
evidence: This is demonstrated by GW4869 treatment experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: Mutant donor cells conferred miR-100-mediated target repression in wild-type-recipient cells in Transwell co-culture experiments.
source: In Transwell co-culture experiments, mutant donor cells conferred miR-100-mediated target repression in wild-type-recipient cells.
evidence: This is supported by luciferase reporter assays shown in Figure 6.

claim: Extracellular miRNAs can function in target cells.
source: These findings suggest that extracellular miRNAs can function in target cells and uncover a potential new mode of action for mutant KRAS in CRC.
evidence: This is inferred from the Transwell co-culture experiments demonstrating functional miRNA transfer.

claim: More than 85% of the reads from the cellular RNA libraries mapped to the genome.
source: Comprehensive sequencing analyses of both cellular and exosomal small RNAs from all three cell lines revealed that more than 85% of the reads from the cellular RNA libraries mapped to the genome, compared to only 50–71% from the exosomal libraries (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is directly shown in the sequencing data analysis presented in Figure 1A.

claim: Only 50–71% of reads from exosomal libraries mapped to the genome.
source: Comprehensive sequencing analyses of both cellular and exosomal small RNAs from all three cell lines revealed that more than 85% of the reads from the cellular RNA libraries mapped to the genome, compared to only 50–71% from the exosomal libraries (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is directly shown in the sequencing data analysis presented in Figure 1A.

claim: The non-mappable reads consisted largely of sequences that contain mismatches to genomic sequences.
source: The non-mappable reads consisted largely of sequences that contain mismatches to genomic sequences.
evidence: This is stated as a result of the sequencing analysis.

claim: In cells, the majority of small RNA reads mapped to microRNAs (miRNAs).
source: In cells, the majority of small RNA reads mapped to microRNAs (miRNAs) (miRbase 19), whereas in exosomes, the majority of small RNA reads mapped to repetitive elements.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B based on annotation of sequencing reads.

claim: In exosomes, the majority of small RNA reads mapped to repetitive elements.
source: In cells, the majority of small RNA reads mapped to microRNAs (miRNAs) (miRbase 19), whereas in exosomes, the majority of small RNA reads mapped to repetitive elements.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B based on annotation of sequencing reads.

claim: Cellular RNA samples displayed an enrichment of miRNA sequences (~70%).
source: Compared to cellular RNA samples, which displayed an enrichment of miRNA sequences (∼70%), miRNA reads in exosomal samples comprised a smaller percentage of the total small reads (5–18%) compared to other ncRNA classes (e.g., tRNAs, rRNAs, snRNAs) (Figure 1B,C, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is quantified from the sequencing data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: miRNA reads in exosomal samples comprised 5–18% of the total small reads.
source: Compared to cellular RNA samples, which displayed an enrichment of miRNA sequences (∼70%), miRNA reads in exosomal samples comprised a smaller percentage of the total small reads (5–18%) compared to other ncRNA classes (e.g., tRNAs, rRNAs, snRNAs) (Figure 1B,C, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is quantified from the sequencing data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The size distribution of cellular small RNA matched that expected from miRNA-derived reads (21–23 nucleotides).
source: The size distribution of cellular small RNA matched that expected from miRNA-derived reads (21–23 nucleotides).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The small RNA read distribution from exosomes was much broader with many reads smaller than 22 nucleotides in length.
source: However, the small RNA read distribution from exosomes was much broader with many reads smaller than 22 nucleotides in length (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: When read identity was restricted to miRNAs by mapping back to known miRNA hairpin sequences, the length distribution of mappable reads was nearly identical between cells and exosomes.
source: Consistent with this, when read identity was restricted to miRNAs by mapping back to known miRNA hairpin sequences, the length distribution of mappable reads was nearly identical between cells and exosomes (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 1D.

claim: Spearman correlation analyses demonstrated high correlation between replicates of individual cell lines (r = 0.95–0.96).
source: Spearman correlation analyses demonstrated high correlation between replicates of individual cell lines (r = 0.95–0.96) and between cellular data sets differing only in KRAS status (r = 0.92–0.96) (Figure 2—figure supplements 1–3).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplements 1–3.

claim: Spearman correlation analyses demonstrated high correlation between cellular data sets differing only in KRAS status (r = 0.92–0.96).
source: Spearman correlation analyses demonstrated high correlation between replicates of individual cell lines (r = 0.95–0.96) and between cellular data sets differing only in KRAS status (r = 0.92–0.96) (Figure 2—figure supplements 1–3).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplements 1–3.

claim: The miRNA profiles from exosomes compared to their parent cells were less correlated (DKO-1 r = 0.67–0.81, DKs-8 r = 0.64–0.71, DLD-1 r = 0.64–0.69).
source: In contrast, the miRNA profiles from exosomes compared to their parent cells were less correlated (DKO-1 r = 0.67–0.81, DKs-8 r = 0.64–0.71, DLD-1 r = 0.64–0.69) (Figure 2—figure supplements 1, 2, 4).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplements 1, 2, 4.

claim: The miRNA profiles from the three cell lines all clustered close to one another.
source: The miRNA profiles from the three cell lines all clustered close to one another indicating that overall miRNA expression profiles are fairly similar among the different cell types (Figure 2).
evidence: This is shown in the principal component analysis in Figure 2.

claim: Exosomal miRNA profiles clearly segregate according to KRAS status.
source: In marked contrast, PC analysis revealed that exosomal miRNA profiles clearly segregate according to KRAS status (Figure 2).
evidence: This is shown in the principal component analysis in Figure 2.

claim: Exosomal miRNA profiles are better predictors of KRAS status than cellular miRNA profiles.
source: Relatively, minor differences between cellular miRNA expression profiles become much more prominent when comparing exosomal miRNA patterns (Figure 2—figure supplement 3). This indicates that the presence of a mutant KRAS allele alters sorting of specific miRNAs to exosomes, a finding that has potentially important implications for biomarker development.
evidence: This is inferred from the principal component analysis showing clearer separation of exosomal samples by KRAS status.

claim: The presence of a mutant KRAS allele alters sorting of specific miRNAs to exosomes.
source: This indicates that the presence of a mutant KRAS allele alters sorting of specific miRNAs to exosomes, a finding that has potentially important implications for biomarker development.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential miRNA profiles observed between wild-type and mutant KRAS exosomes.

claim: For all three cell lines, 25 miRNAs were consistently upregulated in cells.
source: For all three cell lines, 25 miRNAs were consistently upregulated in cells and 29 miRNAs were consistently upregulated in exosomes (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A,B and Tables 1 and 2.

claim: For all three cell lines, 29 miRNAs were consistently upregulated in exosomes.
source: For all three cell lines, 25 miRNAs were consistently upregulated in cells and 29 miRNAs were consistently upregulated in exosomes (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A,B and Tables 1 and 2.

claim: The diversity of miRNAs was substantially greater in mutant KRAS DKO-1 exosomes (94 unique miRNAs) compared to parental DLD-1 or wild-type KRAS DKs-8 exosomes.
source: Additionally, the diversity of miRNAs was substantially greater in mutant KRAS DKO-1 exosomes (94 unique miRNAs) compared to parental DLD-1 or wild-type KRAS DKs-8 exosomes (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3B and Table 2.

claim: Down regulation of miR-100-5p was observed in mutant KRAS DKO-1 and parental DLD-1 cells compared to wild-type KRAS DKs-8 cells.
source: Down regulation of miR-100-5p was observed in mutant KRAS DKO-1 and parental DLD-1 cells compared to wild-type KRAS DKs-8 cells (Table 1).
evidence: This is shown in Table 1.

claim: Decreased miR-100 expression has been shown in metastatic cancers.
source: This is consistent with reports that have shown decreased miR-100 expression in metastatic cancers (Petrelli et al., 2012; Gebeshuber and Martinez, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: miR-100 has been shown to negatively regulate migration, invasion, and the epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT).
source: miR-100 has also been shown to negatively regulate migration, invasion, and the epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT) (Chen et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2014; Zhou et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: miR-100 was enriched in exosomes derived from mutant KRAS cells (>eightfold and >threefold enriched in DKO-1 and DLD-1 exosomes, respectively).
source: Interestingly, miR-100 was enriched in exosomes derived from mutant KRAS cells (>eightfold and >threefold enriched in DKO-1 and DLD-1 exosomes, respectively; Supplementary file 2), suggesting that decrease of miR-100 in cells is due to secretion in exosomes.
evidence: This is shown in Supplementary file 2.

claim: Circulating levels of miR-100 are upregulated in the plasma of mutant KRAS-expressing mouse pancreatic cancer models and in patients with pancreatic cancer.
source: This is in line with findings that circulating levels of miR-100 are upregulated in the plasma of mutant KRAS-expressing mouse pancreatic cancer models and in patients with pancreatic cancer (LaConti et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: miR-10b is preferentially secreted in exosomes isolated from cells harboring a wild-type KRAS allele (>threefold-change and >twofold-change enrichment in DKs-8 and DLD-1 exosomes, respectively).
source: Our RNA sequencing data identified miR-10b as preferentially secreted in exosomes isolated from cells harboring a wild-type KRAS allele (>threefold-change and >twofold-change enrichment in DKs-8 and DLD-1 exosomes, respectively) but retained in mutant KRAS DKO-1 cells (∼threefold-change cell enrichment).
evidence: This is based on RNA sequencing data analysis.

claim: miR-10b is retained in mutant KRAS DKO-1 cells (∼threefold-change cell enrichment).
source: Our RNA sequencing data identified miR-10b as preferentially secreted in exosomes isolated from cells harboring a wild-type KRAS allele (>threefold-change and >twofold-change enrichment in DKs-8 and DLD-1 exosomes, respectively) but retained in mutant KRAS DKO-1 cells (∼threefold-change cell enrichment).
evidence: This is based on RNA sequencing data analysis.

claim: miR-10b is referred to as an oncomiR because it is frequently upregulated during progression of various cancers, including CRC.
source: miR-10b is referred to as an oncomiR because it is frequently upregulated during progression of various cancers, including CRC (Ma, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: miR-320 is aberrantly expressed in several types of cancer, including colon cancer.
source: miR-320 is aberrantly expressed in several types of cancer, including colon cancer.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: miR-320 is expressed in the proliferative compartment of normal colonic crypts.
source: It is expressed in the proliferative compartment of normal colonic crypts (Schepeler et al., 2008; Hsieh et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: miR-320 members (miR-320b, -c, d, and -e) were abundant in both mutant KRAS (DKO-1) and wild-type KRAS (DKs-8) exosomes, but underrepresented in the matched cells.
source: miR-320 members (miR-320b, -c, d, and -e) were abundant in both mutant KRAS (DKO-1) and wild-type KRAS (DKs-8) exosomes, but underrepresented in the matched cells, indicating that some miRNAs are transcribed and predominantly exported into exosomes, independent of KRAS status (Table 2, Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: This is shown in Table 2 and Supplementary file 1A.

claim: miR-320a and miR-320b were the most abundant species represented in exosomes by RNA sequencing analyses.
source: Of these family members, miR-320a and miR-320b were the most abundant species represented in exosomes by our RNA sequencing analyses (miR-320a in DKO-1 exosomes, and miR-320b in DKs-8 and DKO-1 exosomes).
evidence: This is based on RNA sequencing data analysis.

claim: The largest enrichment was observed for miR-320d (fold changes >241 in DKs-8 and >229 in DKO-1) in exosomes relative to cells.
source: Interestingly, however, we observed the largest enrichment for miR-320d (fold changes >241 in DKs-8 and >229 in DKO-1) in exosomes relative to cells, despite being ∼fourfold less abundant than miR-320b levels.
evidence: This is based on RNA sequencing data analysis.

claim: Previous reports have shown differential accumulation of 5p or 3p strands in exosomes compared to parental cells.
source: Previous reports have shown differential accumulation of 5p or 3p strands in exosomes compared to parental cells (Ji et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: For cellular miRNAs, most reads were full length with a slight enrichment in 3′ non-templated addition of A-tailed miRNAs, regardless of KRAS status.
source: For cellular miRNAs, most reads were full length with a slight enrichment in 3′ non-templated addition of A-tailed miRNAs, regardless of KRAS status (Figure 4; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: For exosomes, a slight enrichment for C residues added to the 3′ ends of miRNAs from wild-type KRAS cells was observed.
source: For exosomes, we observed a slight enrichment for C residues added to the 3′ ends of miRNAs from wild-type KRAS cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: An increase in 3′ trimming of miRNAs was noticed in mutant KRAS exosomes.
source: We did not observe this in mutant KRAS exosomes, where instead, we noticed an increase in 3′ trimming of miRNAs (Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Recent evidence suggests that the secretion of miRNAs in exosomes is dependent on ceramide via its production by neutral sphingomyelinase 2 (nSMase 2).
source: Although little is understood regarding the molecular mechanisms for packaging exosomal miRNAs, recent evidence suggests that the secretion of miRNAs in exosomes is dependent on ceramide via its production by neutral sphingomyelinase 2 (nSMase 2) (Kosaka et al., 2010; Mittelbrunn et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Inhibition of de novo ceramide synthesis by treatment with a nSMase inhibitor impaired exosomal miRNA release.
source: Inhibition of de novo ceramide synthesis by treatment with a nSMase inhibitor impaired exosomal miRNA release, apparently due to decreased formation of miRNA-containing exosomes (Kosaka et al., 2010; Mittelbrunn et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: For miR-10b, no significant changes in its cellular levels were observed after treatment with GW4869 in either wild-type KRAS DKs-8 or mutant KRAS DKO-1 cells.
source: For miR-10b, we did not observe significant changes in its cellular levels after treatment with GW4869 in either wild-type KRAS DKs-8 or mutant KRAS DKO-1 cells (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Inhibition of nSMase caused a ∼threefold increase in intracellular levels of miR-100 in mutant KRAS DKO-1 cells but remained unchanged in wild-type DKs-8 KRAS cells.
source: In contrast, inhibition of nSMase caused a ∼threefold increase in intracellular levels of miR-100 in mutant KRAS DKO-1 cells but remained unchanged in wild-type DKs-8 KRAS cells (Figure 5A,B,C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5A,B,C.

claim: miR-320 levels were found to increase (∼2.5 fold) only in GW4869-treated mutant KRAS DKO-1 cells.
source: Similarly, miR-320 levels were found to increase (∼2.5 fold) only in GW4869-treated mutant KRAS DKO-1 cells (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Impaired ceramide synthesis alters cellular accumulation of miRNAs dependent on mutant KRAS.
source: These data are most consistent with the hypothesis that impaired ceramide synthesis alters cellular accumulation of miRNAs dependent on mutant KRAS and suggest that multiple biogenic routes exist for miRNA secretion.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects of GW4869 treatment on miRNA levels in mutant vs wild-type KRAS cells.

claim: Several reports have found that extracellular miRNAs can be taken up by recipient cells to mediate heterotypic cell–cell interactions and facilitate target repression in neighboring cells.
source: Several reports have found that extracellular miRNAs can be taken up by recipient cells to mediate heterotypic cell–cell interactions and facilitate target repression in neighboring cells (Mittelbrunn et al., 2011; Boelens et al., 2014; Squadrito et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Strong Luc repression in the absence of donor cells was observed with perfect MREs (miR-100-PT) compared to the scrambled control (Luc-CTL).
source: Compared to the scrambled control (Luc-CTL), strong Luc repression in the absence of donor cells was observed with perfect MREs (miR-100-PT) (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Significantly increased repression of Luc was observed when the reporter construct containing three perfect miR-100 sites was used in the presence of DKO-1 donor cells.
source: Significantly increased repression of Luc was observed when the reporter construct containing three perfect miR-100 sites was used (miR-100-PT) (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Luc repression was almost completely reversed upon pre-treatment of DKO-1 donor cells with a miR-100 hairpin antagomir inhibitor (AI-100).
source: Luc repression was almost completely reversed upon pre-treatment of DKO-1 donor cells with a miR-100 hairpin antagomir inhibitor (AI-100) (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Cells grown in the presence of donor cells showed an approximate 34% increase in the levels of miR-100.
source: Cells grown in the presence or absence of donor cells showed an approximate 34% increase in the levels of miR-100 (Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Luc-mTOR was significantly repressed in the presence of mutant KRAS DKO-1 but not in the presence of wild-type KRAS DKs-8 donor cells.
source: As observed with miR-100-PT repression, Luc-mTOR was significantly repressed in the presence of mutant KRAS DKO-1 but not in the presence of wild-type KRAS DKs-8 donor cells (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Upon mutation of two MREs (MS2), a partial rescue of Luc expression was observed.
source: However, upon mutation of two MREs (MS2), we observed a partial rescue of Luc expression (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Upon mutation of all three sites (MS3), a complete rescue of miR-100-mediated repressive activity was observed.
source: This was further augmented upon mutation of all three sites (MS3), with a complete rescue of miR-100-mediated repressive activity (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6C.

claim: A greater than twofold repression of the miR-222 Luc reporter was observed in recipient cells.
source: We observed a greater than twofold repression of the miR-222 Luc reporter in recipient cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: Oncogenic KRAS selectively alters the miRNA profile in exosomes.
source: In this study, we comprehensively examined the composition of small ncRNAs from exosomes and cells of isogenic CRC cell lines that differ only in KRAS status. By employing small RNA transcriptome analyses, we found that oncogenic KRAS selectively alters the miRNA profile in exosomes, and that ceramide depletion selectively promotes miRNA accumulation in mutant KRAS CRC cells.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the comprehensive RNA sequencing and analysis.

claim: Ceramide depletion selectively promotes miRNA accumulation in mutant KRAS CRC cells.
source: By employing small RNA transcriptome analyses, we found that oncogenic KRAS selectively alters the miRNA profile in exosomes, and that ceramide depletion selectively promotes miRNA accumulation in mutant KRAS CRC cells.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the GW4869 treatment experiments.

claim: Distinct miRNA profiles between cells and their exosomes may be functionally coupled to mitogenic signaling.
source: Distinct miRNA profiles between cells and their exosomes may be functionally coupled to mitogenic signaling.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion drawn from the observed differences in miRNA profiles.

claim: KRAS status-specific patterns of secreted miRNAs support the idea of using exosomes as potential biomarkers in CRC.
source: KRAS status-specific patterns of secreted miRNAs support the idea of using exosomes as potential biomarkers in CRC.
evidence: This is inferred from the finding that exosomal miRNA profiles segregate by KRAS status.

claim: miR-10b and miR-100 are both part of the miR-10/100 family and differ by only one base in the seed region.
source: miR-10b and miR-100 are both part of the miR-10/100 family and differ by only one base in the seed region, allowing regulation of distinct sets of target mRNAs (Tehler et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: KRAS-dependent differential miRNA expression more prominently affected miRNA expression patterns observed in exosomes than in the parent cells.
source: KRAS-dependent differential miRNA expression more prominently affected miRNA expression patterns observed in exosomes than in the parent cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the principal component analysis showing clearer separation of exosomal samples by KRAS status.

claim: Cells may selectively export miRNAs so as to maintain specific growth or gene expression states.
source: This could reflect a mechanism by cells to selectively export miRNAs so as to maintain specific growth or gene expression states.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the observed differential miRNA export.

claim: Unbound miRNAs that are in excess have the potential to be sorted to exosomes through a 'miRNA relocation effect'.
source: This is consistent with a recent report that found that the cellular levels of miR-218-5p could be maintained, despite changes in the abundance of its target, likely through a 'miRNA relocation effect' where unbound miRNAs that are in excess have the potential to be sorted to exosomes (Squadrito et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: Sequence-specific motifs may direct miRNA trafficking by interaction with specific chaperone proteins.
source: Another mechanism may be through sequence-specific motifs that direct miRNA trafficking by interaction with specific chaperone proteins (Bolukbasi et al., 2012; Villarroya-Beltri et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: The GGAG sequence was not found in other miRNAs that are targeted to exosomes.
source: We found that members of the miR-320 family are preferentially enriched in exosomes independent of KRAS status; however, the GGAG sequence was not found in other miRNAs that are targeted to exosomes.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis of exosomal miRNAs.

claim: The biogenesis of miR-320 family members occurs by a non-canonical pathway that requires neither Drosha nor XPO5.
source: It has been reported that the biogenesis of miR-320 family members occurs by a non-canonical pathway that requires neither Drosha (Chong et al., 2010) nor XPO5 (Xie et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: The 5′ ends of miR-320 family members contain a 7-methyl guanosine cap that facilitates nuclear–cytoplasmic transport through XPO1.
source: Instead, the 5′ ends contain a 7-methyl guanosine cap that facilitates nuclear–cytoplasmic transport through XPO1 (Xie et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: XPO1 is present in DKO-1, DKs-8, and DLD-1 exosomes as detected by mass spectrometry.
source: XPO1 is present in DKO-1, DKs-8, and DLD-1 exosomes as detected by mass spectrometry (Demory Beckler et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: miRNAs in B-cell exosomes display enriched levels of non-template-directed 3′-uridylated miRNAs, while 3′-adenylated miRNA species are preferentially cell enriched.
source: It was recently demonstrated that miRNAs in B-cell exosomes display enriched levels of non-template-directed 3′-uridylated miRNAs, while 3′-adenylated miRNA species are preferentially cell enriched (Koppers-Lalic et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: The addition of non-templated uridine residues to cognate miRNAs accelerates miRNA turnover in certain contexts.
source: In certain contexts, the addition of non-templated uridine residues to cognate miRNAs accelerates miRNA turnover (Baccarini et al., 2011; Wei et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: The stability/half-life of a miRNA may affect whether it is retained or secreted.
source: Thus, it is possible that the stability/half-life of a miRNA affects whether it is retained or secreted.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the observed 3' modifications.

claim: The lack of any apparent motif upon global analysis of miRNAs enriched in exosomes suggests multiple strategies for loading of miRNAs into EVs.
source: However, the lack of any apparent motif upon global analysis of miRNAs enriched in exosomes, coupled to the finding that even untagged miRNAs are differentially exported, suggests multiple strategies for loading of miRNAs into EVs, and that not all EVs and exosomes contain identical cargo.
evidence: This is inferred from the sequence analysis results.

claim: Not all EVs and exosomes contain identical cargo.
source: However, the lack of any apparent motif upon global analysis of miRNAs enriched in exosomes, coupled to the finding that even untagged miRNAs are differentially exported, suggests multiple strategies for loading of miRNAs into EVs, and that not all EVs and exosomes contain identical cargo.
evidence: This is inferred from the heterogeneity observed in miRNA content.

claim: Different cell types secrete a heterogeneous population of vesicles.
source: This further implies that different cell types secrete a heterogeneous population of vesicles.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed differences in exosomal cargo.

claim: The specific sorting of miRNAs into exosomes may enable cancer cells to discard tumor-suppressive miRNAs so as to increase their oncogenic potential.
source: Although the biological relevance of these findings remains to be determined, the specific sorting of miRNAs into exosomes may enable cancer cells to discard tumor-suppressive miRNAs so as to increase their oncogenic potential or perhaps modulate gene expression in neighboring and distant cells to promote tumorigenesis.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the functional significance of differential miRNA export.

claim: miR-100 was found to down-regulate LGR5 in CRC cells and thereby inhibit migration and invasion of such cells.
source: In support of this hypothesis, miR-100, which we found to be enriched in mutant KRAS exosomes, was found to down-regulate LGR5 in CRC cells and thereby inhibit migration and invasion of such cells (Zhou et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: Removal of miR-100 from the cell would be a tumor-promoting event in the context of LGR5 regulation.
source: In this context, removal of miR-100 from the cell would be a tumor-promoting event.
evidence: This is inferred from the known function of miR-100 in inhibiting migration and invasion.

claim: miR-100 can have contradictory activities, both inducing EMT by down-regulating E-cadherin through targeting SMARCA5 and inhibiting tumorigenicity by targeting HOXA1.
source: In other contexts, miR-100 can have contradictory activities, both inducing EMT by down-regulating E-cadherin through targeting SMARCA5 and inhibiting tumorigenicity by targeting HOXA1 (Chen et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: Augmenting miR-100 levels by EV uptake could potentially promote EMT.
source: Thus, although miR-100 can function as a tumor suppressor under normal conditions, augmenting its levels, for example, by EV uptake, could potentially promote EMT.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the potential effects of miR-100 transfer.

claim: miR-100 is part of the miR-125b/let-7a-2/miR-100 cluster that is transcribed and expressed coordinately.
source: Along these lines, miR-100 is part of the miR-125b/let-7a-2/miR-100 cluster that is transcribed and expressed coordinately (Emmrich et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: In malignant colonic tissues from individuals with CRC, miR-100 levels were significantly decreased while let-7a levels were strongly upregulated.
source: Interestingly, in malignant colonic tissues from individuals with CRC, miR-100 levels were significantly decreased while let-7a levels were strongly upregulated (Tarasov et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: miRNAs are secreted from malignant breast epithelial cells after packaging into vesicles larger than conventional exosomes that are enriched in CD44.
source: miRNAs are secreted from malignant breast epithelial cells after packaging into vesicles larger than conventional exosomes that are enriched in CD44, whose expression is linked to breast cancer metastasis (Palma et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: Normal cells tend to release miRNAs in more homogenous types of exosomes.
source: Normal cells tend to release miRNAs in more homogenous types of exosomes, suggesting that malignant transformation may alter the formation of secreted vesicles that could alter miRNA export and lead to differences in exosome content and morphology (Palma et al., 2012; Melo et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: In exosomes from breast cancer cells, CD43 mediates the accumulation of Dicer.
source: In support of this, it was recently shown that in exosomes from breast cancer cells, CD43 mediates the accumulation of Dicer (Melo et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: Exosomes from breast cancer cells contain other RNA-induced silencing complex (RISC) proteins and pre-miRNAs, indicating that miRNA processing can occur in exosomes.
source: These exosomes also contain other RNA-induced silencing complex (RISC) proteins and pre-miRNAs, indicating that miRNA processing can occur in exosomes (Melo et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: Components of the RISC-loading complex were absent in exosomes derived from normal cells.
source: These components were absent in exosomes derived from normal cells.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior published work (Melo et al., 2014).

claim: Quantitative analysis of secreted miRNAs suggested that the levels of extracellular miRNAs are limited.
source: Recently, quantitative analysis of secreted miRNAs suggested that the levels of extracellular miRNAs are limited and raise the question as to how such levels can alter gene expression in recipient cells (Chevillet et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: The full effect of exosomes on recipient cells can be due to a combination of both RNA delivery and protein-based signaling.
source: Our finding that mutant KRAS protein can be functionally transferred in exosomes indicates that the full effect of exosomes on recipient cells can be due to a combination of both RNA delivery and protein-based signaling (Higginbotham et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: Exosomal effects could include activation of Toll-like receptors with possible downstream effects following nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells or mitogen-activated protein kinase cascades.
source: This could include activation of Toll-like receptors with possible downstream effects following nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells or mitogen-activated protein kinase cascades (Fabbri et al., 2012; Chen et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: miR-100 has potential for inhibiting mTOR expression which is required for proliferation of Apc-deficient tumors in mouse models.
source: The complexity of miR-100 function in the tumor microenvironment underscores this argument by its potential for inhibiting mTOR expression which is required for proliferation of Apc-deficient tumors in mouse models (Faller et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: Exosomal transfer of miRNAs might act to select for cells carrying specific tumor driver mutations.
source: In this way, exosomal transfer of miRNAs might act to select for cells carrying specific tumor driver mutations.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the potential role of miRNA transfer in tumor evolution.

claim: Delivery of exosomes to recipient cells can induce cell migration, inflammation, immune responses, angiogenesis, invasion, pre-metastatic niche formation, and metastasis.
source: Our studies have direct implications for CRC and, together with other studies, indicate that delivery of exosomes to recipient cells can induce cell migration, inflammation, immune responses, angiogenesis, invasion, pre-metastatic niche formation, and metastasis (Kahlert and Kalluri, 2013; Boelens et al., 2014; Melo et al., 2014; Costa-Silva et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Exosomes were purified using differential centrifugation and consisted of vesicles ranging in size from 40 to 130 nm.
source: Exosomes were purified using differential centrifugation and consisted of vesicles ranging in size from 40 to 130 nm (Higginbotham et al., 2011; Demory Beckler et al., 2013).
evidence: This describes the methodology used, supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: These preparations exclude larger microvesicles but contain smaller lipoproteins and probably other small RNA–protein complexes.
source: These preparations exclude larger microvesicles but contain smaller lipoproteins and probably other small RNA–protein complexes (unpublished observation).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the methodology.

claim: Exosomes from mutant KRAS DKO-1 cells can be transferred to wild-type cells to induce cell growth and migration.
source: We have previously shown that exosomes from mutant KRAS colorectal cancer (CRC) cells can be transferred to wild-type cells to induce cell growth and migration (Higginbotham et al., 2011; Demory Beckler et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior published work by the authors.

claim: Compared to exosomes derived from isogenically matched wild-type cells, exosomes derived from mutant KRAS cells contain dramatically different protein cargo.
source: Compared to exosomes derived from isogenically matched wild-type cells, exosomes derived from mutant KRAS cells contain dramatically different protein cargo (Demory Beckler et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior published work by the authors.

claim: KRAS status prominently affects the miRNA profile in cells and their corresponding exosomes.
source: Here, we show that KRAS status also prominently affects the miRNA profile in cells and their corresponding exosomes.
evidence: This is the main finding of the current study.

claim: Cellular trafficking of miRNAs is sensitive to neutral sphingomyelinase (nSMase) inhibition in mutant, but not wild type, KRAS cells.
source: Furthermore, we show that cellular trafficking of miRNAs is sensitive to neutral sphingomyelinase (nSMase) inhibition in mutant, but not wild type, KRAS cells and that transfer of miRNAs between cells can functionally alter gene expression in recipient cells.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the GW4869 treatment experiments.

claim: Transfer of miRNAs between cells can functionally alter gene expression in recipient cells.
source: Furthermore, we show that cellular trafficking of miRNAs is sensitive to neutral sphingomyelinase (nSMase) inhibition in mutant, but not wild type, KRAS cells and that transfer of miRNAs between cells can functionally alter gene expression in recipient cells.

claim: KRAS mutations occur in approximately 34–45% of colon cancers.
source: KRAS mutations occur in approximately 34–45% of colon cancers (Wong and Cunningham, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: Small RNAs are thought to be sorted at endosomal membranes.
source: Because small RNAs are thought to be sorted at endosomal membranes and since KRAS signaling can also occur on late endosomes (Lu et al., 2005), we hypothesized that oncogenic KRAS signaling could alter RNA export into exosomes.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: KRAS signaling can occur on late endosomes.
source: Because small RNAs are thought to be sorted at endosomal membranes and since KRAS signaling can also occur on late endosomes (Lu et al., 2005), we hypothesized that oncogenic KRAS signaling could alter RNA export into exosomes.

claim: Mature miRNAs are 21–23 nucleotides in length and bind to target mRNAs to inhibit their expression.
source: Mature miRNAs are 21–23 nucleotides in length and bind to target mRNAs to inhibit their expression (Krol et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Individual miRNAs can potentially regulate hundreds of transcripts within a genome.
source: Because miRNAs imperfectly pair with their mRNA targets, they can potentially regulate hundreds of transcripts within a genome (Bartel and Chen, 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Individual miRNAs exhibit exquisite tissue-specific patterns of expression.
source: However, individual miRNAs exhibit exquisite tissue-specific patterns of expression (Wienholds et al., 2005), control cell fate decisions (Alvarez-Garcia and Miska, 2005), and are often aberrantly expressed in human cancers (Thomson et al., 2006), affording possible disease-specific signatures with diagnostic, prognostic, and therapeutic potential (Lu et al., 2005; Volinia et al., 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: miRNAs have been identified outside the cell in extracellular vesicles (EVs) including exosomes or larger vesicles.
source: In addition to their intracellular roles, recent experiments have identified miRNAs outside the cell in extracellular vesicles (EVs) including exosomes or larger vesicles (Valadi et al., 2007; Crescitelli et al., 2013), in high-density lipoprotein particles (Vickers et al., 2011), or in smaller complexes with Argonaute 2 protein (Arroyo et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Exosomes are small 40–130 nm vesicles of endosomal origin that are secreted by all cells.
source: Exosomes are small 40–130 nm vesicles of endosomal origin that are secreted by all cells and can fuse and be internalized by recipient cells (Valadi et al., 2007; Kosaka et al., 2010; Higginbotham et al., 2011; Mittelbrunn et al., 2011; Montecalvo et al., 2012).

claim: Protein cargo transfer by exosomes between cells is associated with tumor aggressiveness and metastasis.
